Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at evolving wartime tactics from Ukraine and Russia , a new amnesty law in Lebanon , and a deadly ferry disaster in Zimbabwe . “A Unique Operation” Russia and Ukraine traded heavy—and atypical—blows on Tuesday that saw Moscow bombard Ukraine with North Korean ballistic missiles and Kyiv carry out what Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called “ a unique operation ” on a Russian Black Sea naval base. Russia attacked Zaporizhzhia, a city in southeastern Ukraine, with a barrage of missiles supplied by North Korea in an attempt to exploit Ukraine’s critical shortage of Patriot missile interceptors. Over the weekend, Zelensky suggested that Pyongyang could send an additional 50,000 troops to support Moscow’s war effort, reflecting the countries’ deepening ties and Russia’s voracious appetite for manpower. Meanwhile, in a nighttime attack , Ukraine targeted Russia’s naval base in Novorossiysk, nearly 200 miles from the front lines on the far eastern reaches of the Black Sea. Kyiv sent an array of long-range, jet-powered Palianytsia drones; Neptune cruise missiles; and unmanned naval vehicles to target military infrastructure as well as Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, which reportedly retreated from Crimea to Novorossiysk. The drone attack also resulted in Russian civilian deaths, according to the region’s governor, and satellite imagery showed fires at major oil terminals. The Black Sea is again becoming a major front in the war. On Wednesday, Russia claimed an attack on a Ukrainian cargo vessel in the Black Sea, and on Tuesday, the Romanian army reported destroying two Russian drones found floating near Romania’s largest offshore gas project . With attacks on ports and ships, Russia and Ukraine are mutually shutting down the trade routes across the sea, threatening both Russian oil exports and the vast majority of Ukraine’s agricultural exports, Paul Hockenos writes for Foreign Policy . Russian President Vladimir Putin, who was overseeing naval drills in the country’s far east on Wednesday, also issued a warning to Europe. If European states continue to “plunder” commercial vessels containing Russian cargo—referring to recent seizures of ships suspected to belong to Russia’s illegal shadow fleet —Moscow will be “forced to respond in kind,” he said. Retaliation would come “wherever we ourselves ​deem it necessary and appropriate.” Already, these aggressive strategies from both Kyiv and Moscow are expanding the war beyond the deadlocked front lines—at the cost of surging civilian deaths. Although Ukraine says it has handed U.S. negotiators proposals to end the war, analysts (and Zelensky himself ) are skeptical that Russia wants anything but escalation. A report from the Institute for the Study of War on Monday concluded: “Ukraine’s Patriot shortages offer Russia an opportunity to cause very serious damage to Ukraine over the coming winter and will therefore contribute to delaying meaningful negotiations and protracting the war.” Today’s Most Read Why China’s Elites Still Want to Leave by Yaqiu Wang What Morocco Was Saying to Spain in Ceuta by Albert Guasch Rafael China Has Chosen to Disappoint Its Consumers by Charles Sun and Christopher Nye What We’re Following Amnesty in Lebanon. Lebanon’s parliament passed two landmark bills this week designed to revamp the country’s criminal justice system. On Tuesday, the parliament voted to abolish the death penalty, becoming the first country in the Middle East to officially end capital punishment. Although Lebanon hasn’t carried out an execution since 2004 , courts continued to hand out death sentences for offenses such as espionage, murder, and terrorism. Lebanon now joins more than 100 other countries that have formally abolished the death penalty for all crimes. And on Wednesday, the country’s parliament passed a controversial and long-debated amnesty law meant to reduce overcrowding in prisons. Under the law, inmates detained without charges for more than 12 “prison years” (a prison year is defined as nine months) will be released while their trials continue. The law will also reduce sentences for certain crimes, including killing Lebanese troops and some forms of drug dealing; free some convicted militants; and allow Lebanese citizens who fought Hezbollah and later fled to Israel to return to Lebanon. Intense debate over the bill has inflamed the country’s sectarian tensions, with Sunnis, Shiites, and Christians seeking amnesty for prisoners from their own communities. Opponents of the bill, including families of slain Lebanese soldiers, say the political bargains and sweeping amnesty fall short of real institutional reform. Ferry disaster. A ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe on Tuesday, killing 44 people. The ship had a carrying capacity of just 90 people, but Zimbabwe’s disaster management agency says that at least 114 adult passengers and five crew members were on board, and possibly as many as 153 . The government-owned vessel ferries people between rural communities on the shore of the lake to the northern town of Kariba. A witness told AFP that the boat departed in bad weather and may have been hit by a rogue wave; other witnesses told state broadcaster ZBC that the captain dismissed passengers’ urges to turn back. President Emmerson Mnangagwa declared a state of disaster , as search and rescue operations continue. Seventy-seven people have been rescued so far. However, it remains unclear how many people may be still missing, as the total count of passengers onboard excludes potential passengers who had not bought tickets as well as children under ticketing age. Turning a new leaf. András Baka, the former president of the Hungarian Supreme Court, was elected president of Hungary by the country’s parliament on Tuesday in a vote of 140 to 6. His appointment follows the resignation in July of former President Tamás Sulyok, who agreed to step down after Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s ruling Tisza party passed a constitutional amendment to end his term. Before the vote to elect Baka, all 51 lawmakers belonging to former Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s Fidesz party walked out of the chamber in protest of Sulyok’s ousting. The role of president in Hungary is largely ceremonial, but Baka’s appointment comes with a great deal of symbolism. Orban removed Baka from his role as president of the Supreme Court in 2011, three years before his term was supposed to expire—a decision later found unlawful by the European Court of Human Rights. When Magyar defeated Orban in April, he took power with “a mandate to dismantle a competitive authoritarian system 16 years in the making,” David Koranyi wrote for Foreign Policy . Still, many have wondered whether the prime minister—who has passed 27 laws and two constitutional amendments so far—can restore democracy without resorting to undemocratic means. After the vote, Baka told the parliament that the country’s future “demands both justice and ​self-restraint.” “We cannot build the new Hungary on revenge,” he said. Odds and Ends French cnidarians seem to have an agenda. For the second consecutive Aug. 10, “ several dozen tons ” of swarming jellyfish blocked pumping systems at a French nuclear plant, forcing parts of the facility to go offline. Jellyfish swarms have become more common along the French coast in recent years due to rising sea temperatures. Despite the mighty efforts of multiple fishing vessels to keep the creatures at bay over the weekend, they were eventually overrun. However, Électricité de France, the government-owned utility company that operates the plant, said that the situation has not impacted the safety of the facilities, personnel, or environment. Photograph: George Walker IV/AP Mississippi Mississippi police say more arrests to come in death of woman found hanging from tree Officials still investigating death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman, a day after man’s arrest in relation to killing Associated Press Sat 12 Sep 2026 13.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Mississippi police said on Saturday they were still investigating the death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree last month, a day after a man was arrested in connection with the killing. Loved ones also painted a picture of Fortune as a mother, athlete and woman of faith who they hoped would not solely be remembered for her horrific death. Police sought and found Jarques Ratliff, 51, who is Black, and arrested him when they encountered him walking on the street, authorities said on Friday. Jackson’s police chief, RaShall Brackney, also said on Friday that additional arrests are expected in the case. Ratliff should appear in Jackson municipal court no later than Monday morning, said André de Gruy, Mississippi’s state defender. Brackney said Ratliff had an “association” with Fortune but would not elaborate on their relationship. She said police arrested Ratliff on a homicide charge and called that “an important development” in the investigation. “But it is not the conclusion. This case remains active, and additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence wherever it leads,” Brackney said on Friday. “We understand that this case has received media attention from across the globe, and across this community.” The state medical examiner’s office determined on Thursday evening that the death was a homicide, Brackney said, allowing police to execute the warrants they already had on hand. Police did not respond to calls and messages from the Associated Press on Saturday about potential updates to the investigation beyond confirming it was still going on. Ratliff also did not appear in Hinds county jail records on Saturday. It couldn’t immediately be determined if he had a lawyer, and a message was left for the public defender’s office. If represented by a public defender, it would be the Hinds county public defender, de Gruy said. Man arrested over death of Mississippi woman found hanging from a tree Read more Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, said on Friday after police told her of the arrest: “I just started crying and told them, ‘Thank you, thank you, thank you.’” Spivey said police did not share a motive or whether DNA led them to the arrest. Spivey said she did not know the man who had been arrested, but she was asking her daughter’s friends if they knew him. Spivey described the family as “in disbelief” and “shock”. “We still don’t have a lot of answers,” Spivey said. Police discovered Fortune’s body hanging in the backyard of an abandoned home in Jackson on 3 August. Spivey said she was certain that her daughter, 29, would not have killed herself. “Absolutely not. Even if she could climb that tree, no, no, she would never, ever, ever,” Spivey said. An obituary about Fortune posted on the website of Tucker funeral home in Central City, Kentucky, in August stated that Fortune’s “path was not always easy, and there were highs and lows”. It also stated that she skipped her junior year of high school, was a star cross-country runner, and had a strong faith in God. Services were held last month in Kentucky . “She leaves behind a powerful legacy of resilience, rooted deeply in her unwavering faith. Even in her darkest hours, she never stopped believing in her Savior,” the obituary stated. Fortune was also the mother of four children, but she rarely saw two of them, Spivey said. The last time Spivey saw her daughter was in late July for a planned family reunion in Kentucky that was canceled, but her daughter came to see her anyway. “When she was there, there was this pull, like a spiritual pull to her. I needed her. I guess God knew that was going to be it,” Spivey said. Spivey said she and Fortune’s father faced racism and violence as a mixed-race couple in Crittenden county, Kentucky, before Fortune was born. Fortune was taken from her parents and placed in foster care as a child. During her high school years, she moved around among group homes and eventually ran away to Mississippi. The obituary stated that she had lived in Jackson for 10 years. Spivey wasn’t sure where Fortune was living at the time of her death but said her daughter had been struggling with homelessness in recent years. Fortune had two sisters and was close with them. The father of one of her children was verbally and physically abusive to Fortune, Spivey said. Before she died, Fortune had talked about starting a cleaning business and was trying to get her life in order. “Say her name. Keep it going,” Spivey said. “Because I’m not going to stop until I get answers.” Explore more on these topics Mississippi US crime US policing news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.dw.com/en/zelenskyy-accuses-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ORg7 Zelenskyy has accused Washington of deliberately stalling arms deliveries Image: Henry Nicholls/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the US administration of delaying the delivery of crucial missiles needed by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks . He told US senators on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" even though they had already been paid for by Ukraine's European allies. The accusations come as Ukraine-US relations are strained. US President Donald Trump has eased sanctions on Russia and directly criticized Zelenskyy, calling for someone else to take his place. What did Zelenskyy say? The Ukrainian president said that the US was holding back interceptor missiles , with one shipment only waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth before it could be sent to Ukraine. He also said that Ukraine's European allies had agreed to transfer some of their own Patriot missiles but that this too was pending the green light from the US . "The missiles are ready, and they could already be in Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "But unfortunately, there is still no approval." Ukraine urgently needs more air defence missiles like the Patriot system Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS Earlier on Monday, he said Ukraine had again not received any early warnings about incoming Russian missile strikes. The country is dependent on the ability of US intelligence to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles fired by Russia. There are also growing concerns over restrictions affecting Starshield, a military satellite communications network developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Ukrainian military communications and drone operations depend on using Starshield data. The US government controls access to Starshield, but Trump has denied ordering any restrictions. US says it's not withholding intelligence The accusations come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure. In the night between Sunday and Monday, several Russian ballistic missiles struck the Ukrainian capital and its surroundings , cutting off electricity to more than half a million households. "Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram about the attack. The US, though, dismissed claims it was withholding information, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisting that Washington had not paused its intelligence sharing with Kyiv. Regarding the easing of sanctions and the diesel deal between Washington and Moscow , Donald Trump strongly criticized Zelenskyy for calling out the deal. "Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said on Monday. "To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."
